"""Permission classes for the billing API.

These answer "may this account call this endpoint at all". They deliberately do
not implement ``has_object_permission``: a permission class that scoped objects
would only run on detail routes, and list routes would still leak. Scoping the
queryset is the only place that covers both, so that is where it belongs.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from rest_framework.permissions import BasePermission

BILLING_ROLES = ("owner", "billing_admin")


class IsOrganizationMember(BasePermission):
    message = "This account is not a member of any organization."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        user = request.user
        return bool(user and user.is_authenticated and getattr(request, "tenant", None) is not None)


class IsBillingAdmin(BasePermission):
    message = "Billing administrator access is required."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        if request.method in ("GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"):
            return True
        membership = request.user.memberships.filter(organization=request.tenant).first()
        return membership is not None and membership.role in BILLING_ROLES

"""Tenant resolution.

``TenantMiddleware`` runs after authentication and attaches the caller's
organization to the request as ``request.tenant``. It resolves the tenant; it
does not scope anything. Every queryset that touches a customer-owned table is
responsible for filtering on ``request.tenant`` itself, because the ORM has no
idea a request is in progress.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from django.utils.functional import SimpleLazyObject
from rest_framework.exceptions import PermissionDenied

from billing.models import Organization


def _resolve(request) -> Organization | None:
    user = getattr(request, "user", None)
    if user is None or not user.is_authenticated:
        return None
    membership = user.memberships.select_related("organization__plan").first()
    if membership is None:
        raise PermissionDenied("This account is not a member of any organization.")
    return membership.organization


class TenantMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        request.tenant = SimpleLazyObject(lambda: _resolve(request))
        return self.get_response(request)

"""Permission classes for the billing API.

These answer "may this account call this endpoint at all". They deliberately do
not implement ``has_object_permission``: a permission class that scoped objects
would only run on detail routes, and list routes would still leak. Scoping the
queryset is the only place that covers both, so that is where it belongs.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from rest_framework.permissions import BasePermission

BILLING_ROLES = ("owner", "billing_admin")


class IsOrganizationMember(BasePermission):
    message = "This account is not a member of any organization."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        user = request.user
        return bool(user and user.is_authenticated and getattr(request, "tenant", None) is not None)


class IsBillingAdmin(BasePermission):
    message = "Billing administrator access is required."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        if request.method in ("GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"):
            return True
        membership = request.user.memberships.filter(organization=request.tenant).first()
        return membership is not None and membership.role in BILLING_ROLES

"""Tenant resolution.

``TenantMiddleware`` runs after authentication and attaches the caller's
organization to the request as ``request.tenant``. It resolves the tenant; it
does not scope anything. Every queryset that touches a customer-owned table is
responsible for filtering on ``request.tenant`` itself, because the ORM has no
idea a request is in progress.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from django.utils.functional import SimpleLazyObject
from rest_framework.exceptions import PermissionDenied

from billing.models import Organization


def _resolve(request) -> Organization | None:
    user = getattr(request, "user", None)
    if user is None or not user.is_authenticated:
        return None
    membership = user.memberships.select_related("organization__plan").first()
    if membership is None:
        raise PermissionDenied("This account is not a member of any organization.")
    return membership.organization


class TenantMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        request.tenant = SimpleLazyObject(lambda: _resolve(request))
        return self.get_response(request)

"""Permission classes for the billing API.

These answer "may this account call this endpoint at all". They deliberately do
not implement ``has_object_permission``: a permission class that scoped objects
would only run on detail routes, and list routes would still leak. Scoping the
queryset is the only place that covers both, so that is where it belongs.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from rest_framework.permissions import BasePermission

BILLING_ROLES = ("owner", "billing_admin")


class IsOrganizationMember(BasePermission):
    message = "This account is not a member of any organization."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        user = request.user
        return bool(user and user.is_authenticated and getattr(request, "tenant", None) is not None)


class IsBillingAdmin(BasePermission):
    message = "Billing administrator access is required."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        if request.method in ("GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"):
            return True
        membership = request.user.memberships.filter(organization=request.tenant).first()
        return membership is not None and membership.role in BILLING_ROLES

"""Tenant resolution.

``TenantMiddleware`` runs after authentication and attaches the caller's
organization to the request as ``request.tenant``. It resolves the tenant; it
does not scope anything. Every queryset that touches a customer-owned table is
responsible for filtering on ``request.tenant`` itself, because the ORM has no
idea a request is in progress.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from django.utils.functional import SimpleLazyObject
from rest_framework.exceptions import PermissionDenied

from billing.models import Organization


def _resolve(request) -> Organization | None:
    user = getattr(request, "user", None)
    if user is None or not user.is_authenticated:
        return None
    membership = user.memberships.select_related("organization__plan").first()
    if membership is None:
        raise PermissionDenied("This account is not a member of any organization.")
    return membership.organization


class TenantMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        request.tenant = SimpleLazyObject(lambda: _resolve(request))
        return self.get_response(request)

"""Permission classes for the billing API.

These answer "may this account call this endpoint at all". They deliberately do
not implement ``has_object_permission``: a permission class that scoped objects
would only run on detail routes, and list routes would still leak. Scoping the
queryset is the only place that covers both, so that is where it belongs.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from rest_framework.permissions import BasePermission

BILLING_ROLES = ("owner", "billing_admin")


class IsOrganizationMember(BasePermission):
    message = "This account is not a member of any organization."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        user = request.user
        return bool(user and user.is_authenticated and getattr(request, "tenant", None) is not None)


class IsBillingAdmin(BasePermission):
    message = "Billing administrator access is required."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        if request.method in ("GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"):
            return True
        membership = request.user.memberships.filter(organization=request.tenant).first()
        return membership is not None and membership.role in BILLING_ROLES

"""Tenant resolution.

``TenantMiddleware`` runs after authentication and attaches the caller's
organization to the request as ``request.tenant``. It resolves the tenant; it
does not scope anything. Every queryset that touches a customer-owned table is
responsible for filtering on ``request.tenant`` itself, because the ORM has no
idea a request is in progress.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from django.utils.functional import SimpleLazyObject
from rest_framework.exceptions import PermissionDenied

from billing.models import Organization


def _resolve(request) -> Organization | None:
    user = getattr(request, "user", None)
    if user is None or not user.is_authenticated:
        return None
    membership = user.memberships.select_related("organization__plan").first()
    if membership is None:
        raise PermissionDenied("This account is not a member of any organization.")
    return membership.organization


class TenantMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        request.tenant = SimpleLazyObject(lambda: _resolve(request))
        return self.get_response(request)

"""Permission classes for the billing API.

These answer "may this account call this endpoint at all". They deliberately do
not implement ``has_object_permission``: a permission class that scoped objects
would only run on detail routes, and list routes would still leak. Scoping the
queryset is the only place that covers both, so that is where it belongs.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from rest_framework.permissions import BasePermission

BILLING_ROLES = ("owner", "billing_admin")


class IsOrganizationMember(BasePermission):
    message = "This account is not a member of any organization."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        user = request.user
        return bool(user and user.is_authenticated and getattr(request, "tenant", None) is not None)


class IsBillingAdmin(BasePermission):
    message = "Billing administrator access is required."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        if request.method in ("GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"):
            return True
        membership = request.user.memberships.filter(organization=request.tenant).first()
        return membership is not None and membership.role in BILLING_ROLES

"""Tenant resolution.

``TenantMiddleware`` runs after authentication and attaches the caller's
organization to the request as ``request.tenant``. It resolves the tenant; it
does not scope anything. Every queryset that touches a customer-owned table is
responsible for filtering on ``request.tenant`` itself, because the ORM has no
idea a request is in progress.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from django.utils.functional import SimpleLazyObject
from rest_framework.exceptions import PermissionDenied

from billing.models import Organization


def _resolve(request) -> Organization | None:
    user = getattr(request, "user", None)
    if user is None or not user.is_authenticated:
        return None
    membership = user.memberships.select_related("organization__plan").first()
    if membership is None:
        raise PermissionDenied("This account is not a member of any organization.")
    return membership.organization


class TenantMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        request.tenant = SimpleLazyObject(lambda: _resolve(request))
        return self.get_response(request)

"""Permission classes for the billing API.

These answer "may this account call this endpoint at all". They deliberately do
not implement ``has_object_permission``: a permission class that scoped objects
would only run on detail routes, and list routes would still leak. Scoping the
queryset is the only place that covers both, so that is where it belongs.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from rest_framework.permissions import BasePermission

BILLING_ROLES = ("owner", "billing_admin")


class IsOrganizationMember(BasePermission):
    message = "This account is not a member of any organization."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        user = request.user
        return bool(user and user.is_authenticated and getattr(request, "tenant", None) is not None)


class IsBillingAdmin(BasePermission):
    message = "Billing administrator access is required."

    def has_permission(self, request, view):
        if request.method in ("GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"):
            return True
        membership = request.user.memberships.filter(organization=request.tenant).first()
        return membership is not None and membership.role in BILLING_ROLES

"""Tenant resolution.

``TenantMiddleware`` runs after authentication and attaches the caller's
organization to the request as ``request.tenant``. It resolves the tenant; it
does not scope anything. Every queryset that touches a customer-owned table is
responsible for filtering on ``request.tenant`` itself, because the ORM has no
idea a request is in progress.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from django.utils.functional import SimpleLazyObject
from rest_framework.exceptions import PermissionDenied

from billing.models import Organization


def _resolve(request) -> Organization | None:
    user = getattr(request, "user", None)
    if user is None or not user.is_authenticated:
        return None
    membership = user.memberships.select_related("organization__plan").first()
    if membership is None:
        raise PermissionDenied("This account is not a member of any organization.")
    return membership.organization


class TenantMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        request.tenant = SimpleLazyObject(lambda: _resolve(request))
        return self.get_response(request)

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; GET /v1/shipments assembles its WHERE clause from whichever console filters arrived, then runs it with database/sql.
cases.why: Every other filter appends its value to args and emits a $n placeholder, but the free-text `q` parameter is formatted directly into the predicate text with fmt.Sprintf and then concatenated into the statement that QueryContext executes. A single quote in `q` closes the ILIKE literal, so the caller controls the rest of the WHERE clause and can UNION in any table the API role can read, across every tenant. The tenant_id binding on lines 52-53 is correct and does nothing to help, because the injected text is appended after it.

cases.architecture: chi v5 router; GET /v1/shipments/lookup assembles its WHERE clause from whichever scan-gun filters arrived, then runs it with database/sql.
cases.why: The statement is still built by fmt.Sprintf and strings.Join over a dynamic clause list, which is exactly the shape of its vulnerable sibling, but every Sprintf here formats only a placeholder index: the scanned term travels as the value "%"+q+"%" in args and the predicate text only ever says $n. The ORDER BY column comes from lookupSortColumns, so the caller's sort key indexes a map of fixed column literals and is then discarded, and LIMIT/OFFSET are bound rather than interpolated. No caller-controlled byte reaches the statement text.

cases.why: The handler proves the caller is authenticated and then never uses that fact: the row is selected on `WHERE s.id = $1` alone, with the actor's TenantID not in the predicate. Shipment ids are opaque but they are handed out in search results, webhooks and label keys, so any signed-in operator on any tenant can read another tenant's consignee name, address and declared value by substituting the id. The query even scans tenant_id into the response body, which makes the missing comparison plain.

cases.why: The event query really is scoped by id alone — `WHERE e.shipment_id = $1` with no tenant column, because tracking_events has none — which looks identical to the defect in its sibling. It is correct because assertShipmentVisible has already resolved the same id against `shipments WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2` using the actor from the context, and returns ErrNotFound for a shipment on another tenant, so the handler cannot reach the second query with an id it is not entitled to.

cases.why: The `key` query parameter is joined onto the spool root and opened with no confinement check. filepath.Join normalises ".." rather than rejecting it, so key=../../../../etc/passwd resolves outside the spool and the file is streamed back with Content-Disposition attachment. The comment's assumption — that the key was minted by the renderer — is not enforced anywhere, and the key arrives from the client on every request. Any authenticated operator gets arbitrary read of whatever the service account can open, including every other tenant's labels.

cases.why: The caller-supplied key is still passed straight into filepath.Join with the spool root, which is the same construct that makes its sibling exploitable. It is safe because resolveInsideSpool never returns the joined path directly: it resolves both the root and the candidate through EvalSymlinks and then requires filepath.Rel(root, candidate) not to be ".." or to start with "../", so anything that climbs out of the spool — including a symlink planted inside it — is reported as a 404 before os.Open is reached.

# frozen_string_literal: true

module Api
  module V1
    # Every v1 controller hangs off this one.
    #
    # The seller console is a browser client on a sibling origin, so its session
    # rides in a signed HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie; the mobile clients present
    # the same opaque token as a bearer header instead. Either way we store only
    # the digest, so a database dump hands nobody a live session.
    class BaseController < ActionController::API
      include ActionController::Cookies

      class Unauthenticated < StandardError; end

      before_action :authenticate_seller!

      rescue_from Unauthenticated do
        render json: { error: "unauthenticated" }, status: :unauthorized
      end

      rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound do
        render json: { error: "not_found" }, status: :not_found
      end

      rescue_from ActionController::ParameterMissing do |error|
        render json: { error: "invalid_request", parameter: error.param }, status: :bad_request
      end

      private

module Api
  # Turns "this record exists" into "this record is yours".
  #
  # A controller includes this *after* the callback that loads its member record,

    # does not exist, so ids stay unenumerable.

      record = instance_variable_get(:"@#{controller_name.singularize}")
      raise ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound if record.nil?
      raise ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound unless record.seller_id == Current.seller.id
    end
  end
end

# Prepares a parameter hash for an application log line.
#
# The list is an allow-list rather than a deny-list on purpose: a field nobody

    form_kind country_code region_code locale consent_version
    submitted_from entity_type has_dependents

cases.why: Every other privileged method on this controller carries @PreAuthorize("hasRole('RECORDS_ADMIN')"), but the disposition sweep added in 4.3 has none, and the controller deliberately sits on /api/v1/retention-policies rather than under the /api/v1/admin prefix that the filter chain restricts. cases.why: The handler starts from the same tempting shape — annotations.findById(annotationId) straight off a path variable, with no scope in the query. It is safe because the two statements after it settle ownership: the resolved annotation's document must match the documentId in the path, and DocumentAccessPolicy#requireViewer throws AccessDeniedException unless the document is in the caller's workspace and the caller owns it or holds an inherited folder grant. The check cannot be folded into the repository predicate without reimplementing the folder-grant walk in JPQL, which is why it is a separate call.

cases.why: The SQL is assembled by string concatenation into a StringBuilder across four conditional branches, which is the shape that usually signals injection. Every interpolated fragment is a ? placeholder though, and the user's value goes into the args list — including the LIKE patterns, where the % wildcards are concatenated onto the argument rather than into the statement. The only non-parameterisable fragment, the ORDER BY column, is looked up in the SORT_COLUMNS map and the request is rejected outright when the key is unknown, so nothing from the request ever reaches the statement text.

cases.why: A user-supplied relative path is joined onto a filesystem root and streamed back, which is the vulnerable shape almost exactly. It is correct because the root is canonicalised once in the constructor with toAbsolutePath().normalize(), and the resolved candidate is proven to sit inside it with file.startsWith(templateRoot) before anything opens it — a traversing name resolves and normalizes happily and is then rejected by that comparison. Ordering is what makes it work: the containment proof happens after resolution, so it cannot be defeated by encoding.

cases.why: allowedOriginPatterns("*") combined with allowCredentials(true) tells Spring to reflect whatever Origin the browser sends back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and to permit the session cookie with it. Unlike allowedOrigins("*"), that combination is not rejected at startup, so it ships silently. The mapping covers the whole authenticated /api/v1/** surface with allowedMethods("*"), so any page a user visits can read and write every document in their workspace with their own credentials.

cases.architecture: Spring Boot 3 REST API for an enterprise document-management product: @RestController handlers, Spring Data JPA repositories, JdbcTemplate read models for reporting, and one Spring Security filter chain with method security enabled.
cases.why: allowedOrigins("*") is right there in the mapping, which is the construct the sibling gets wrong. It is safe for two reasons that have to be read together: allowCredentials is explicitly false, so no browser will attach the session cookie to a cross-origin call, and the mapping is scoped to /api/v1/public/**, which ApiSecurityConfiguration marks permitAll() — a record-class dictionary and MIME glossary that an anonymous curl can already fetch. Methods are restricted to GET and HEAD, so there is nothing to forge either.

cases.why: The request body carries a base64 blob and the handler feeds it to ObjectInputStream.readObject() with no filter. Java deserialization constructs whatever the stream names before any cast is evaluated, so the (DesktopLayout) cast and the ClassCastException catch below it run far too late to help; a gadget chain from any library on the classpath executes during readObject. The size cap bounds memory, not classes. Any user who can authenticate can reach it, and the fix is an ObjectInputFilter allow-list rather than better validation of the result.

cases.why: This is the same legacy Java-serialization endpoint, base64 blob and readObject() included, so it looks identical to the sibling. The difference is the line before the read: setObjectInputFilter installs a JEP 290 allow-list naming only the four data-only state classes plus String, Integer, Number, Enum, UUID and ArrayList, terminated by !* so every other class is refused before its constructor or readObject runs. The same filter caps depth, refs, array length and byte count, which closes the resource-exhaustion path that an allow-list alone leaves open.
